summary: Describes practices for letting an authoritative name server operator provide one named server at multiple locations through shared unicast (anycast) addresses, improving distribution and reducing query latency. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3258 explains how a DNS operator can place several copies of one authoritative name server around the network and give them all the same address, so a query reaches the copy nearest to the asker. Each copy keeps a second, private address for administration and for receiving zone files. The memo also explains what breaks: the copies must change over at the same time, and connections that need many packets can be split between copies.

subtitle: How one authoritative name server can be reached from many places without changing routing

tldr.problem: One named authoritative name server sits in one place, so users far from it get slow answers and a single local problem takes the service down for them.
tldr.mechanism: The operator gives the same IPv4 address to several copies of the server, keeps each copy on a second, private administrative address, and uses BGP so that traffic for the shared address is delivered to the nearest copy.
tldr.outcome: The copies answer from more of the network and with less latency, and a denial-of-service attack or a cut fibre now costs the operator a fraction of the service. The price is coordination: the copies must be switched over in step, and a shared address confuses TCP traffic.

facts.label: Interfaces per host
facts.value: 2: the shared unicast interface and an administrative interface

facts.label: Routing protocol used
facts.value: BGP, with the operator's own autonomous system number

facts.label: Address space needed
facts.value: None beyond the shared unicast address

facts.label: IP version covered
facts.value: IPv4 only; IPv6 is for further study

today: RFC 3258 is an Informational memo from April 2002 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It records a set of operational practices for spreading authoritative name servers, and states that applicability to IPv6 was left for further study.

sections.title: Sharing One Server Across Many Places
sections.content:
The memo describes a set of practices intended to enable an authoritative name server operator to provide access to a single named server in multiple locations. The primary motivation is to increase the distribution of DNS servers to previously under-served areas of the network topology and to reduce the latency for DNS query responses in those areas.

The document presumes a one-to-one mapping between named authoritative servers and administrative entities, that is, operators. It contains no guidelines or recommendations for caching name servers. The shared unicast system described here is specific to IPv4; applicability to IPv6 is an area for further study. The system is related to the one described in RFC 1546, but it does not require dedicated address space, routing changes, or the other elements of a full anycast infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is to put copies of one authoritative name server in more places, so that people far from the original get quicker answers. It is an IPv4 practice, and it deliberately avoids the extra machinery that full anycast would need.

sections.title: How the Mesh Is Built
sections.content:
In addition to being configured properly as a standard authoritative name server, each host taking part in a shared-unicast system should be configured with two network interfaces. These may be two physical interfaces, or one physical interface mapped to two logical interfaces. One of the network interfaces should use the IPv4 shared unicast address associated with the authoritative name server. The other interface, referred to as the administrative interface, should use a distinct IPv4 address specific to that host. The host should respond to DNS queries only on the shared-unicast interface, and it is good practice to limit the responses on that interface to zones for which the host is authoritative.

Zone files should be delivered to the administrative interface, to minimise the risk of man-in-the-middle attacks, and secure file transfer methods with strong authentication should be used for all transfers. If the hosts in the mesh make their zones available for zone transfer, the administrative interfaces should be used for those transfers as well, in order to avoid the problems with potential routing changes for TCP traffic.

Authoritative name servers may be loosely or tightly synchronised, depending on the practices set by the operating organisation. Switch-overs from one data set to another should be coordinated as much as possible. The use of synchronised clocks on the participating hosts, and set times for switch-overs, provides a basic level of coordination. A more complete coordination process would involve receipt of zones at a distribution host, confirmation of the integrity of the zones received, distribution of the zones to all of the servers in the mesh, confirmation of the integrity of the zones at each server, coordination of the switchover times for the servers in the mesh, and a failure process that ensures servers that did not receive correct data, or could not switch over to the new data, cease to respond to incoming queries until the problem can be resolved. Depending on the size of the mesh, the distribution host may also be a participant, and for authoritative servers it may also be the host on which zones are generated.

The memo does not advise that routes be withdrawn in the case of failure. It advises instead that the DNS process shut down, so that servers on other addresses are queried. This reflects a choice between performance and operational complexity: withdrawing the route for a specific server instance when it is not available is possible, but ensuring that this happens reliably is operationally complex, and given the existing DNS failover methods the marginal improvement in performance will not justify the extra complexity for most uses.

Server placement should emphasise diversity in the network topology, which is the driving force behind these practices, rather than geographic diversity alone, which merely reduces the effects of service disruptions due to local problems. Ideally, servers should be placed topologically near the points at which the operator exchanges routes and traffic with other networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Each copy of the server has two addresses: the shared one that the public uses, and a private one for administration. Zone files arrive on the private address, and all the copies switch to new data at the same moment. Copies should sit in different places in the network, not merely different cities.

sections.title: Routing and the Split-Destination Problem
sections.content:
The organisation administering the mesh of servers sharing a unicast address must have an autonomous system number and speak BGP to its peers. To those peers, the organisation announces a route to the network containing the shared-unicast address of the name server. The organisation's border routers must then deliver the traffic destined for the name server to the nearest instantiation. Routing to the administrative interfaces for the servers can use the normal routing methods for the administering organisation.

One potential problem with using shared unicast addresses is that routers forwarding traffic to them may have more than one available route, and those routes may in fact reach different instances of the shared unicast address. Applications like DNS, whose communication typically consists of independent request-response messages each fitting in a single UDP packet, present no problem. Other applications, in which multiple packets must reach the same endpoint, such as TCP, may fail or present unworkable performance characteristics in some circumstances. Split-destination failures may occur when a router does per-packet or round-robin load sharing, or when a topology change occurs that changes the relative metrics of two paths to the same anycast destination.

Four things mitigate the severity of this problem. UDP is a fairly high proportion of the query traffic to name servers. The aim of the proposal is to diversify topological placement, and for most users the coordination of placement means that new instances of a name server are at a significantly different cost metric from existing instances, so only some users end up in the middle, and that should be relatively rare. Per-packet load sharing is only one of the possible load sharing mechanisms, and other mechanisms are increasing in popularity. Lastly, in the case where the traffic is TCP, per-packet load sharing is used and equal-cost routes to different instances are available, any DNS implementation that measures the performance of servers to select a preferred server will quickly prefer a server for which the problem does not occur.

For the DNS failover mechanisms to reliably avoid the problem, those using shared unicast distribution must take care that all of the servers for a specific zone are not participants in the same shared-unicast mesh. Organisations implementing these practices should always provide at least one authoritative server which is not a participant in any shared unicast mesh. Any specific host may become unreachable to a client should a server fail, a path fail, or the route to that host be withdrawn, but these error conditions are not specific to shared-unicast distributions and would occur for standard unicast hosts. Since ICMP response packets might go to a different member of the mesh than that sending a packet, packets sent with a shared unicast source address should also avoid using path MTU discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator announces the shared address with BGP so that traffic arrives at the nearest copy. A single DNS query is fine because it is one small packet. A longer conversation can break, because the router may send some packets to one copy and others to another.

sections.title: Administration
sections.content:
A single point of contact for reporting problems is crucial to the correct administration of this system. If an external user of the system needs to report a problem related to the service, there must be no ambiguity about whom to contact. If internal monitoring does not indicate a problem, the contact may of course need to work with the external user to identify which server generated the error.

Appendix A of the memo contains an ASCII diagram of an example of a simple implementation of this system. In it, the odd numbered routers deliver traffic to the shared-unicast interface network and filter traffic from the administrative network, while the even numbered routers deliver traffic to the administrative network and filter traffic from the shared-unicast network. These are depicted as separate routers for the ease that gives in explanation, but they could easily be separate interfaces on the same router. A local NTP source is depicted for synchronisation, but the level of synchronisation needed would not require that source to be either local or a stratum one NTP server.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone must be the single address people report problems to, because a user cannot tell which copy of the server answered them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As a core piece of Internet infrastructure, authoritative name servers are common targets of attack. The practices outlined here increase the risk of certain kinds of attacks and reduce the risk of others.

The architecture increases the number of physical servers, which could increase the possibility that a server mis-configuration will occur and allow a security breach. In general, the entity administering a mesh should ensure that patches and security mechanisms applied to a single member of the mesh are appropriate for, and applied to, all of the members. Genetic diversity, meaning code from different code bases, can be a useful security measure in avoiding attacks based on vulnerabilities in a specific code base; in order to ensure consistency of responses from a single named server, however, that diversity should be applied to different shared-unicast meshes, or between a mesh and a related unicast authoritative server.

The level of systemic synchronisation should be augmented by synchronisation of the data present at each of the servers. While DNS itself is a loosely coupled system, debugging problems with data in specific zones would be far more difficult if two different servers sharing a single unicast address might return different responses to the same query. For example, if the data associated with a domain has changed and the administrators of the domain are testing for the changes at the authoritative name servers, they should not need to check each instance of a named authoritative server. The use of NTP to provide a synchronised time for switch-over eliminates some aspects of this problem, but mechanisms to handle failure during the switchover are required: a server which cannot make the switchover must not roll back to a previous version, it must cease to respond to queries so that other servers are queried.

If the mechanism used to distribute zone files among the servers is not well secured, a man-in-the-middle attack could result in the injection of false information. Digital signatures will alleviate this risk, but encrypted transport and tight access lists are a necessary adjunct to them. Since zone files are distributed to the administrative interfaces of meshed servers, the access control list for distribution of the zone files should include the administrative interface of the server or servers, rather than their shared unicast addresses.

On the other side, the increase in the number of physical servers reduces the likelihood that a denial-of-service attack will take out a significant portion of the DNS infrastructure. It also reduces the effect of machine crashes, fibre cuts and localised disasters, by reducing the number of users dependent on a specific machine.
sections.plainLanguage: More copies spread the damage a hacker or a broken cable can do, but they also multiply the places a mistake can be made. Every copy must be patched the same way, must hold the same data, and must take zone files only over an encrypted, tightly controlled channel.

viz.caption: WHAT MORE COPIES OF A SERVER COST AND WHAT THEY BUY

cells: More chances of a misconfiguration; patches and security mechanisms must be applied to every member of the mesh
Two copies sharing one address could answer the same query differently, which makes faults hard to debug
A man-in-the-middle could inject false information unless transfers are encrypted and access lists are tight
A denial-of-service attack, machine crash or fibre cut now takes down a smaller share of the service
